account: Voters in New Hampshire received an AI-generated robocall impersonating President Biden before the 23 January 2024 primary. On 25 January 2024 Pindrop, a company that builds synthetic-audio detection tools, published its analysis of a 39-second clip on its website. Pindrop checked the clip's patterns against more than 120 voice synthesis engines. Its chief executive, Vijay Balasubramaniyan, told WIRED that the result came back well north of 99 percent for ElevenLabs. Hany Farid's team at the University of California, Berkeley, was initially skeptical and ran its own model on the same sample. The team concluded with high confidence that the audio was AI-generated and likely made with ElevenLabs. ElevenLabs' own detector returned 84 percent, a result that WIRED reproduced. New Hampshire Public Radio reported on 23 May 2024 that the New Hampshire Attorney General had announced 26 charges against Steven Kramer. It also reported that the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) had proposed a $6 million fine. The sources do not connect the state charges to Pindrop's analysis. On 24 May 2024 the FCC stated in its proposed fine against Kramer that the robocall had been made with software from a website run by Eleven Labs. For that statement it cites Pindrop's analysis and an NBC News report. A New Hampshire jury acquitted Kramer of the state charges on 13 June 2025. Kramer told the Associated Press that he would not pay the FCC's fine.

ai_role.statement: Pindrop's system made the attribution, and Hany Farid's Berkeley team reached the same result with its own model. The FCC later stated the same fact; for it, the FCC cites Pindrop's post and an NBC News report in which the magician says that he used ElevenLabs. The system's contribution was an early public attribution that the magician's account and the regulator later matched.
